chapter_theme: Sivavakkiyar's fiercest run against rite and rule: stone images, dawn and dusk bathing, 'our god and your god', the sacred thread, menstrual and birth pollution, caste, flesh and leavings. His one argument is turned on each in turn: every body, Brahmin or Saiva, grew from blood and the pollution they call impure, and the Lord did not stand apart from flesh; so purity is nowhere outside and the Lord is nowhere but within. Beside the attack stand the inner worship (feet as linga, breath as thread), the cipher of the mandalas in which the Lord dances, and the counsel to stop wanting.
structure_note: Cipher verses open and close (1089, 1090, 1106 to 1108); between them the polemic runs by topic: stone gods and bathing (1093, 1094), sects (1095), pollution and caste in a connected run (1096 to 1101), scripture (1103, 1104, 1110), flesh (1111, 1112) and leavings (1113). 1102 on wanting and 1109 on the guru's word stand apart.

1089.reading: One can stay, one can stay on earth; one can push away even the seven worlds of Hari, Mal and Brahma; in the pit that takes no embryo, in the pillar without legs, once the fire-chamber has been opened, you and I are the Lord.
1089.nuance: The pit that does not conceive and the legless pillar are coded: tradition reads the root centre and the central channel, and நெருப்பறை, the fire-chamber, as the kundalini fire. On that reading the verse promises long life on earth and mastery over the worlds, then union. 'You and I' may be the poet and the Lord, or the poet and a disciple.

1090.reading: Having become single enjoyment, the two becoming one, how do enjoyment and union still fit? When becoming and perishing have both become its concern, there is no dying and no being born, none, none at all.
1090.nuance: ஏகபோகம், single enjoyment, is 1053's term; the two who become one are read as Siva and Shakti, or the two breaths. The question of line 2 is rhetorical: once two are one there is nothing left to unite. அதன்கண் நேயம் is unclear, 'the aim in it' or 'love in it'.

1091.reading: If, with the four Vedas as the elements and the water that mingles there, and with the feet as the linga, one does worship in devotion, the jnanis who open the final door from the ear and cut the bond pass beyond beginning and end and reach the rare release.
1091.nuance: An inner puja: the Vedas as the elements, water as the bath, the feet (the Lord's or one's own) as the linga. காதினின்று கடைதிறந்து, opening the end from the ear, is obscure; perhaps the guru's word in the ear opens the last door. The verse does not condemn worship, it relocates it.

1092.reading: Men who twist cotton thread and recite 'cotton': if you can twist the thread of the bellows and end sorrow, the book in the mind turns to art and the book of time passes away; the five letters Sivaya set the book right and end care.
1092.nuance: If பருத்திநூல், the cotton thread, is the sacred thread of the twice-born, the verse sets against it துருத்திநூல், the thread of the bellows, the breath drawn in the lungs; நூல் is also 'book', so the twisting of thread and the reading of books collapse into one word. காலநூல், the book of time or fate, is what the breath undoes. The reading of line 1 is not secure.

1093.reading: Mute ones who perform the dying rites of the tattvas: can gods become stone? What can I do but laugh? The first shoot of the three-eyed one, whom the three gods cannot know, stays mingled within you as your guard; look.
1093.nuance: சாவதான தத்துவச் சடங்கு, rites of tattvas that die: rites addressed to perishable matter. The question தேவர் கல்லும் ஆவரோ can be 'can gods be stone?' or 'can stones be gods?'; either way the image is denied and the Lord is placed within as காவல், the guard.

1094.reading: Fools who plunge into water morning and evening: what did the frog that lay in the water morning and evening gain? If you rise in good time and think of the root with one of your three eyes, release and attainment come.
1094.nuance: The frog is the reductio: a creature that lives in the holy water gains nothing by it. கண்கள் மூன்றில் ஒன்று, one of the three eyes, is the inner eye at the brow; மூலம், the root, is the Lord or the base centre. 1105 takes up the morning-and-evening of this verse.

1095.reading: Our god and your god: are there two gods? Are there two gods, one there and one here? Is not the first form that stands there and here one? Those who speak sect-quarrel will die with their mouths rotting with worms.
1095.nuance: வங்கவாரம் is unclear, taken as partisan talk or crooked speech. The curse is as fierce as the argument is simple: a god with a location (அங்கும் இங்கும்) is not the first form.

1096.reading: Of what lay between the rooms you say 'that day is impure'; when one is born in the proper order you say 'that day is impure'; when one knows the ford and bathes you say 'that day is impure'; how can one join with base men without forbearance?
1096.nuance: தூமை is ritual pollution, chiefly menstrual and birth pollution; the three cases are the woman secluded (அறையறை இடை, in the inner room), the birth, and the bath that is supposed to end it. The verse opens the run 1096 to 1101, in which pollution is shown to be the source of every body. Line 1 and line 3 are not secure.

1097.reading: That water stood in and came from the space where sound arose; fools who, maddened, writhe and sink in water: what is purity? What is the rule? What is it that stood seen as cleanness? What is the madman's body that came to be, and what difference, O wisdom?
1097.nuance: சத்தம் வந்த வெளி, the space from which sound came, is the first element in the order of evolution; water is a late derivative of the same space, so no purer than what it washes. கட்டு may be the rule, the bond or the knot. The questions are left as questions.

1098.reading: Month by month it is pollution, and the pollution that was forgotten; was it not when the months ceased that the form grew? What nada, what Veda, what good castes? Say how the Veda-reciting Brahmins came to be!
1098.nuance: The argument is biological: the embryo forms when the monthly blood stops, so the body of every Brahmin is made of what he calls impure. 'Forgotten pollution' may be the blood that did not flow because it became the child. The verse asks for a genealogy and expects none.

1099.reading: Was it when pollution ceased that the good lamp stood? Was it when maleness ceased that custom ceased? When lowness ceased and maleness ceased and agitations ceased, in the time when pollution upon pollution ceased, speech ceased and stood.
1099.nuance: A ladder of negations (அற்று) ending in the cessation of speech. தூமை and ஆண்மை may be the female and male principles whose ceasing is the state beyond; தாண்மை is unclear (தாழ்மை, lowness, or தன்மை, nature). சுதீபம், the good lamp, is the light that stands when all this is gone.

1100.reading: Fools who speak of the oozing pollution and the life settled in it as two different things: how then did it come to be? Is it not the stinking pollution that becomes the good castes? Raging fool, that is the shape in which pollution stood.
1100.nuance: The verse closes the gap the purity rules depend on: the life cannot be held apart from the blood it settled in, and the high castes are that blood grown up. நின்ற் in the last line is a broken form.

1101.reading: From the oozing pollution of the woman who saw her trouble, man and woman joined everywhere in the land and the world came to be; the life that had renounced, with pollution itself as its desire: which land is the land that stands free of pollution?
1101.nuance: தீமை கண்டு நின்ற பெண், the woman who saw her trouble, is the woman at her period, as the next line's union shows. Line 3 is hard: the renounced life (சீவன்) that takes pollution as its desire may be the soul drawn back into birth, or the renouncer whose body is still the same blood. The final question has no answer: there is no such country.

1102.reading: Saying 'I want, I want', you wander in vain seeking; though you seek wanting, there is nothing but what is; once you renounce the longing that seeks saying 'I want', the very thing you wanted is quickly seen.
1102.nuance: The verse keeps the object: what was wanted is seen, not dissolved, once the wanting stops. உள்ளதல்லது இல்லையே, there is nothing other than what is, makes the seeking itself the obstacle.

1103.reading: The Vedas the twice-born recite, the excellent Agamas, the firmly set causes and the true books declared, the teaching tied up and kept and all the madness fit for stories: all of it ended as dust once I had known the Lord.
1103.nuance: The list is careful to include the true books (மெய்ம்மை நூல்கள்) with the stories: the point is not that scripture is false but that it ends (முடிந்ததே) at knowledge. பிரானை யான் அறிந்தபின் makes it a report of the poet's own case.

1104.reading: A hundred crore Agamas, a hundred crore mantras, recited for a hundred crore days: what use is that? Six and six and six, and within the heart the one letter: recite the rising excellent letter and the Lord comes and speaks.
1104.nuance: ஆறும் ஆறும் ஆறும் is not keyed; eighteen, or the six adharas counted three ways. The one letter is the pranava or the seed of the five letters. The verse does not reject recitation; it reduces its object from crores to one.

1105.reading: Death who stands mingled in morning and evening: tell me, what is the maya by which evening becomes morning and reddens? If, free of morning and evening, you subside into thought, the Death who stood as morning and evening is not, is not.
1105.nuance: காலன் is Time and Death at once, and morning and evening are both the passage of days and the twice-daily rites of 1094. So the verse reads two ways: escape time by settling in thought, or give up the dawn-and-dusk observance and settle in thought; both end the Death that the alternation is.

1106.reading: Within the eight mandalas, bending two mandalas; within the set mandala, counting, six mandalas; in the mandala touched, appearing, three mandalas; within the mandala of the dance the Lord stood dancing.
1106.nuance: The counts eight, two, six, three are given without a key; tradition reads mandalas as the regions of sun, moon and fire and as the centres of the body. நட்டமண்டலம் may be the fixed (நட்ட) mandala or the mandala of the dance (நட்டம்). 1107 asks the question this verse answers.

1107.reading: Within the eight mandalas, where does the Lord stand? At the two legs, the root channel: there Rudra was seen; the two fish-eyes mingling, the eight directions closed, the upper two mingling, he stood swinging and dancing.
1107.nuance: The question is placed inside the body: the root channel at the legs, the eyes, the eight directions (the senses or the petals), and the upper two (the brows, or the two channels joined above). Which 'two' and which 'eight' is cipher; what is plain is that the dance is located within.

1108.reading: Mother, father, salt water: what is known you do not know; mother, father, salt water became Hari, Ayan and Aran; once mother, father, salt water became the first of the first, nothing became anything but you, mother-father.
1108.nuance: உப்புநீர், salt water, is read in tradition as the parental fluids, the seed and blood of generation; the verse climbs from them to the three gods and to the First, and ends in the one addressed as mother-father. The attack of 1096 to 1101 continues under cipher: the same fluids make gods and men.

1109.reading: Before taking form, how did the body join together? Before conceiving, how were the causes? How does the awareness set in it fit? Mark the word the guru set right, understand it and take it in.
1109.nuance: Three questions about what precedes the body, and no answer but the guru's word. The verse admits that the body's origin is not settled by argument, after a run of verses that argue it from blood.

1110.reading: There is a beginning and no end; then there were no four Vedas; there is light and no word, and nothing that has passed beyond words; the breath that sat in the first three, who knew even itself at the beginning, O Lord?
1110.nuance: The Vedas are set after the beginning, so not eternal. சொல்லிறந்தது ஏதுமில் may mean nothing beyond words exists, or nothing of what passes words can be told. ஆதியான மூவர் are Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra or the three letters; the breath seated in them is the breath of 1056.

1111.reading: 'Flesh, flesh, flesh', you say, speaking follies; how did our Lord stand apart from flesh? As flesh, as babbling, as the one of great name who walks about, the madman who sprouted in flesh: see, he is the Father.
1111.nuance: The target is the horror of flesh as impure, and 1112's 'Saiva fools' suggests vegetarian Saivas. The argument is not that eating is good but that the Lord is in flesh and grew in it; whether that defends eating it is left to the hearer. பித்தன், the madman, is Siva's own epithet.

1112.reading: You drank milk made from blood and grew with it; what was one and other became two, one may say; what is it you cast off as drink, and what is this 'flesh and meat'? What grew into the frame, Saiva fools?
1112.nuance: Mother's milk is blood transformed, so the body was fed on blood from the start; the Saiva who refuses flesh is made of it. மதிரமாக விட்டதேது is unclear, perhaps 'what did you set aside as intoxicant' (மதுரம், sweet, is another reading). The verse asks what the rejected flesh differs from, and answers with the body itself.

1113.reading: The stone that has eaten you throw away saying 'leavings'; are the leavings you see not of the hand, or is it different for the Supreme? Listen about the leavings you see: in the water mingled by the hand, what purity did you get? Fools without insight!
1113.nuance: உண்ட கல் is hard: the stone image that has 'eaten' the offering, after which the food is எச்சில் (leavings), or the vessel one ate from. பாணி is hand or water; the hand that purifies is itself unclean, and the water used has touched mouths. On either reading the rule of leavings is turned on the one who keeps it.

links.note: Tirumular turns the one who blazes at the root opening upward with the breath and burns Death in the yoga of fire; Sivavakkiyar opens the fire-chamber in the pit that takes no embryo and can then stay on earth and push the worlds aside. Both read the fire at the root as the way past death.

Both make the puja inward: Tirumular's heart is the temple, the soul the linga and the senses the lamps; Sivavakkiyar's elements are the Vedas, water the bath and the feet the linga. In both the rite is kept and its objects replaced.

Tirumular says curd, ghee, copper, fire, brick, bilva or gold, any one of them clearly known, can be the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar asks whether gods can be stone and can only laugh. The conflict holds if Tirumular means the material object is to be worshipped as Siva; if தெளிவுறக் கண்டு means that knowing makes any thing the linga, Sivavakkiyar's Lord 'mingled within you' is not far from it.

Tirumular says the Lord is a cow of stone to those who stand apart without knowing him; Sivavakkiyar says stone cannot be god at all and the Lord is the guard within. Tirumular's stone is what the Lord becomes for the unknowing; Sivavakkiyar's is what the knowing should never have mistaken.

Tirumular: those who know only bathing cannot join him, he is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. Sivavakkiyar: the frog that lives in the water gains nothing, think of the root with the inner eye. Both set inner thought against the bath and keep the bath's goal.

Tirumular: kin is one and God is one, and there is no refuge outside one's own mind; Sivavakkiyar: there are not two gods, ours and yours, since the first form is one here and there. Both make the oneness of God a reproach to sect.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are only words, and austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar asks 'what good castes?' and demands to be told how the Brahmins came to be. Both empty the word; the Naladiyar refills it with conduct, Sivavakkiyar with blood.

Tirumular assigns the linga's material by varna, crystal for Brahmins, gold for kings, komalam for Vaishyas, bana stone for Shudras; Sivavakkiyar says every caste is the same monthly blood grown into a body and asks what good castes there are. The conflict holds if Tirumular's rule treats varna as a real difference in worship; if it only records custom without ranking it, as its own text allows, the two can stand together.

1075 lists caste among the forms the one origin took; 1100 gives the mechanism, the oozing pollution that grows into the good castes, and refuses to let the life be spoken of apart from the blood it settled in.

The Kural says that giving up craving at once yields a nature that does not shift; Sivavakkiyar says that once the wanting is renounced the thing wanted is quickly seen. Both make the gain immediate on the dropping of the want, though the Kural's gain is a state and Sivavakkiyar's is a sight.

Tirumular says recitation is not needed once the Life of life has come within; Sivavakkiyar says Vedas, Agamas and true books ended as dust once he knew the Lord. Both put scripture before knowledge in time and after it in worth.

Tirumular's fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas and, once known, become the five; Sivavakkiyar's hundred crore Agamas and mantras are useless beside the one letter within. Both compress scripture into a letter, Tirumular to five and Sivavakkiyar to one.

Tirumular says the twenty thousand eight hundred kinds of karma, mantra and yoga only tire the body and come down to four; Sivavakkiyar says a hundred crore Agamas recited for a hundred crore days are no use beside one letter. The reduction is the same gesture at a different number.

1094 mocks the dawn-and-dusk bathers; 1105 turns their காலைமாலை into காலன், Death that is the alternation of morning and evening, and says settling in thought beyond both ends him. The rite's hours become the thing to escape.

Tirumular's yogi seeks the Lady dancing where there is neither night nor day and becomes a child that age does not touch; Sivavakkiyar's practitioner, free of morning and evening and settled in thought, has no Death. Both place the deathless state outside the alternation of day and night.

1106 gives the counts of mandalas and says the Lord dances in the mandala of the dance; 1107 asks where in the eight he stands and answers with places in the body, the root channel at the legs, the eyes, the closed directions, the upper two.

1103 says scripture ended as dust once the Lord was known; 1110 goes further back and says that at the beginning there were no four Vedas at all, only light and no word. Scripture is late in time as well as spent in use.

Tirumular says none but those who eat having put flesh away can reach the Lord's feet, whatever their offerings; Sivavakkiyar says calling flesh impure is folly since the Lord sprouted in flesh and never stood apart from it. The conflict holds if 1111 defends eating flesh, as 1112's address to Saivas suggests; if it only denies that flesh is apart from God, Tirumular's rule of abstention is untouched.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh, and hell will not release the eater; Sivavakkiyar says the Saiva who rejects flesh grew on milk made of blood and is flesh himself, so the rejection is folly. The conflict holds if 1112 is a defence of eating; the Kural's ground is the killed creature and Sivavakkiyar's is the eater's own body, so each leaves the other's reason unanswered.

1096 turns the rule of pollution on its keepers, who find impurity in seclusion, birth and the bath alike; 1113 turns the rule of leavings on them, since the purifying hand and water are themselves leavings. The same move on two rules.

1098 asks how the Veda-reciting Brahmins came to be, since every body grew when the monthly blood stopped; 1111 asks how the Lord could stand apart from flesh. One argument, from the body's origin, applied to caste and to the horror of flesh.

source_issues: 1092: பஞ்சி ஓதும் in line 1 is unclear and may be corrupt for a word meaning 'recite'.
1099: தாண்மை is not a standard form (தாழ்மை or தன்மை).
1100: நின்ற் at the end of line 4 is broken, probably நின்ற.
1112: மதிரமாக is unclear (மதுரமாக or a word for drink).
